analysis.one_liner: Extends workplace breastfeeding break and privacy protections to salaried workers currently left out.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, markup, or vote: it was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee on the day it was introduced and expired with the 117th Congress in January 2023, having drawn 7 Republican cosponsors and no Democratic ones.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the federal labor law that governs wages and hours so that salaried and other workers not covered by existing breastfeeding rules get a reasonable break and a private, non-bathroom space to express milk for one year after a child's birth. It puts the protections in the same enforcement framework as wage rules, and directs the Government Accountability Office to report to Congress on how the accommodations are implemented and expanded.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing mothers in jobs not covered by existing federal law — mainly salaried 'exempt' employees such as managers and professionals — would gain a right to reasonable break time and a private place, other than a bathroom, to express milk for one year after their child's birth.

how_it_helps.text: Extends existing workplace protections for nursing mothers to salaried employees and other types of workers not covered under current law.
Requires covered employers to provide reasonable break time and a place other than a bathroom that is shielded from view and free from intrusion, for one year after a child's birth.
Time spent expressing breast milk must count as hours worked if the nursing mother is also working during that time.
Directs the GAO to report to Congress on how many working mothers gained access to accommodations, what employers implemented, and how the Labor Department enforces the rules.

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers, who must provide break time and a private space for nursing employees; the break time is generally unpaid except when the employer requires active work during it, and businesses with fewer than 50 employees can be exempted if compliance would be an undue hardship.

drawbacks.text: Employers are not required to pay employees for breastfeeding break time, except to the extent the employer requires active work during the break.
Employers with fewer than 50 employees are exempt if the requirements would impose a significant difficulty or expense relative to the size, resources, or structure of the business.
An employer that is notified it is not in compliance is deemed not to have violated the rule if it fixes the problem within 30 days of notice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core value is real: it closes a gap that left salaried workers — disproportionately teachers, nurses, and professionals — without any federal right to a break or a private space, at a modest and largely one-time cost to employers for space and scheduling. The design is softer than its title suggests, though: the breaks are unpaid, small businesses can claim a hardship exemption, and a 30-day fix-it window limits penalties, so the protection is a floor rather than a guarantee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 1, 2021, and referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — was recorded for the rest of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have newly owed accommodation duties — particularly those employing salaried workers outside current protections — avoided the requirement, while nursing mothers in those jobs entered 2023 still without a federal right to break time or a private space.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers not yet covered by break rules

for.name: Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Supporting Working Mothers Act on July 1, 2021.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after the bill was referred to it; no hearing, markup, or vote was scheduled.

against.name: Rep. Robert C. 'Bobby' Scott
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 7 cosponsors were Republicans, no Democrats cosponsored, and the Democratic-run committee never acted, so no vote ever showed where either party stood.

industries.note: These employers would newly owe nursing mothers break time and a private, non-bathroom space — a compliance duty the bill would have applied for the first time to jobs now exempt. Their interest in avoiding the requirement runs against the workers it would protect.
The bill carries forward an exemption for businesses with fewer than 50 employees when compliance would be an undue hardship, keeping the new requirements off them.
